sentences.text: The genus Dromornis includes extinct flightless birds known as mihirungs, which resemble modern ostriches or emus but possess greatly reduced wings and large legs. The name Dromornis comes from Ancient Greek words meaning 'course' or 'race' and 'bird', reflecting their terrestrial nature. These birds belong to the family Dromornithidae, a group of extinct flightless birds.
Although they look like giant emus, Dromornis is more closely related to early waterfowl of the Anseriformes order or a basal galliform.
The mass of Dromornis australis is estimated to range from 133 to 208 kg, while Dromornis stirtoni could reach up to 650 kg. Dromornis murrayi stood about 1.5 meters high and weighed up to 250 kg.
Dromornis planei had a stocky build and was as large as an ostrich or emu. It featured a curved, deep bill and a remarkably large head and skull.
Dromornis stirtoni could reach a weight of 650 kg, making it one of the largest birds to ever exist.
Dromornis planei possessed a remarkably large head and skull equipped with a curved, deep bill.
The Aboriginal Tjapwuring people called these giants 'mihirung paringmal', a term meaning 'giant bird'.

The genus Dromornis was described by Richard Owen in 1872, with the type species being Dromornis australis. The type specimen of this species was a femur found in a 55-meter well at Peak Downs, Queensland, and described by Owen in 1872.

A large femur fossil was discovered at Peak Downs, Queensland, at a depth of about 55 meters in a well shaft. The species Dromornis australis is known from a right femur approximately twelve inches long found at Peak Downs.

Dromornis murrayi was described in 2016 based on fossils found among the Riversleigh fauna in Queensland, Australia. Patricia Vickers-Rich first described Dromornis planei in 1979, initially placing it in the genus Bullockornis.
Patricia Vickers-Rich first discovered Dromornis stirtoni in 1979 in the Alcoota Fossil Beds in the Northern Territory of Australia.

Dromornis species were likely predominantly or exclusively herbivorous browsers. While some researchers considered Dromornis planei carnivorous due to its large shearing beak, most currently agree it was a herbivore. Gastroliths found with Dromornis planei suggest a herbivorous diet, though some suggestions propose it had carnivorous abilities similar to terror birds. It is widely accepted that Dromornis stirtoni was herbivorous.

Dromornis stirtoni likely existed alongside other dromornithids and browsing marsupials as an apex herbivore. There is a debate regarding diet, but it is widely accepted that Dromornis stirtoni was mostly herbivorous, possibly occasionally scavenging or eating smaller prey.

The parent group of Dromornis is Dromornithidae. In 2010, Nguyen and Boles suggested that Bullockornis is a species of Dromornis based on skeletal traits and phylogenetic analyses, a view supported by subsequent studies.
Dromornis species lived in Australia from the Oligocene to the Pliocene epochs.

Fossils of Dromornis australis are found in Pliocene deposits in Australia. Dromornis murrayi lived during the Oligocene to early Miocene and is the earliest known species of the genus. Fossils of Dromornis murrayi at the Riversleigh Hiatus site date to the early Miocene and the late Oligocene to early Miocene.
Dromornis planei fossils are found in the Bullock Creek fauna in the Northern Territory of Australia.
It is debated whether Dromornis planei is related to geese and ducks or to Galliformes, with some studies supporting the latter.

Despite the accepted herbivorous diet, various indicators suggest Dromornis stirtoni may have been carnivorous or omnivorous. Various factors are proposed to have contributed to the extinction of Dromornis stirtoni. Murray and Vickers-Rich suggested Dromornis stirtoni went extinct because it was out-competed for food sources due to dietary overlap with other large animals.
It is debated whether Dromornis was a carnivore, with recent researchers suggesting its beak size implies a carnivorous diet.
